context: they all thought in chorus (I hope you understand what thinking in chorus means
mainIdea: The voices in the train carriage think as a group that Alice should say nothing. They say that language costs a lot of money.
simple: Alice thought to herself, "Then there is no use in speaking." This time the voices did not join in, because she had not spoken. But to her great surprise they all thought together, like a chorus. The writer says he hopes you understand what thinking in chorus means, but he must say that he does not. They thought, "It is better to say nothing at all. Language is worth a thousand pounds a word!"

context: only think how convenient it would be if you could manage to go home without it
mainIdea: The Gnat says it would be easy for Alice to lose her name. Then the governess could not call her to lessons.
simple: The Gnat went on in a careless voice. He said that he did not know, and told Alice to think how easy it would be if she could go home without her name. For example, if the governess wanted to call Alice to her lessons, she would call out "come here" and then she would have to stop, because there would be no name for her to call. Then, of course, Alice would not have to go.

context: This must be the wood,” she said thoughtfully to herself, “where things have no names
mainIdea: Alice thinks about losing her name in the wood where things have no names. She thinks it would be funny but also a little bad.
simple: Alice says this must be the wood where things have no names. She wonders what will happen to her own name when she goes in. She would not like to lose it, because they would have to give her another, and it would almost surely be an ugly one. But then the fun would be in trying to find the creature that has her old name. She says it is like the notices when people lose dogs, which say that the dog answers to the name of Dash and had on a brass collar. She says to think of calling everything you met Alice until one of them answered. But she says they would not answer at all, if they were wise.

context: if it was so, it might be; and if it were so, it would be
mainIdea: Tweedledee answers with the opposite idea. He says what would be if it were so, and says it is not so. He calls this logic.
simple: Tweedledee said, on the other side, that if it was so, it might be, and if it were so, it would be. But as it is not so, it is not. He said that is logic.

context: But answer came there none — And that was scarcely odd, because
mainIdea: This is the last part of the poem. The Carpenter asks the oysters to go home, but no oyster answers, because they have all been eaten.
simple: The Carpenter said, "O Oysters, you have had a pleasant run! Shall we be trotting home again?" But no answer came. That was hardly strange, because the Walrus and the Carpenter had eaten every one.

context: “If that there King was to wake,” added Tweedledum, “you’d go out —bang!
mainIdea: Tweedledum says that Alice would disappear like a candle if the Red King woke up.
simple: Tweedledum added that if the King woke, Alice would go out with a bang, just like a candle.

context: The rule is, jam tomorrow and jam yesterday —but never jam today
mainIdea: The Queen says there is jam on the day before and the day after, but never on the day you are in.
simple: The Queen said that Alice could not have jam even if she wanted it. She said the rule is jam tomorrow and jam yesterday, but never jam today.

context: things that happened the week after next
mainIdea: The Queen remembers things that have not happened yet. She talks about a messenger who is punished before his trial.
simple: The Queen answered in a careless voice that she remembers things that happened the week after next. For example, she said, and she stuck a large piece of plaster on her finger as she spoke, the King's Messenger is in prison now, being punished. His trial does not even begin until next Wednesday. And of course the crime comes last of all.

context: sometimes I’ve believed as many as six impossible things before breakfast
mainIdea: The Queen says that she has had a lot of practice at believing impossible things.
simple: The Queen said she supposed Alice had not had much practice. She said that when she was Alice's age, she always did it for half an hour a day. She said that sometimes she had believed as many as six impossible things before breakfast. Then she cried that there goes the shawl again.
